title: Search Closed Sources: Purchase Technical Data
shortTitle: Search Closed Sources: Purchase Technical Data
summary: This sub-technique covers buying technical facts about a specific target rather than reading analysis about a sector. The goods are concrete: employee contact lists, credential dumps taken from unrelated breaches, network diagrams, remote access details, and scan output for a chosen address range. Sellers range from legitimate paid aggregation services to criminal marketplaces that specialise in stolen data. The purchase happens outside the victim estate, so the trails are payment records, marketplace accounts, and vendor audit logs, none of which the victim holds. What a defender does see is the aftermath: authentication attempts with valid-looking usernames, password reset abuse, or phishing that references internal project names. Matching those signs against known breach disclosures usually explains where the data came from.

beginner.definition: This sub-technique is about buying facts rather than reading reports. The facts may include staff email addresses, old passwords, or details of your network. Sellers include paid data services and criminal markets. It differs from the parent because the attacker pays for specific technical detail about a target.
beginner.whyItMatters: Bought credentials and contact lists make attacks much cheaper to run. A single valid password can open a remote login without any exploit. Staff lists make phishing messages look genuine because names and roles are correct. You cannot block a purchase that happens elsewhere. You can reduce the damage by watching for logins that use old or reused passwords.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a seller that advertises the kind of data they need.
They buy a dataset, for example an address range scan or a credential list.
They check whether the data relates to their chosen target and how recent it is.
They enrich it with free public details, such as job titles from social media.
They use valid accounts or send tailored messages that reference real names.
They may resell the data, which spreads the exposure to other attackers.
beginner.example: Imagine a market stall that sells second-hand keys, and each key carries a paper tag with a street name. A thief buys every tag that says your street. They do not need to pick the lock if one key still fits. Bought technical data is that box of keys. Your building did nothing wrong and saw nothing at all.
takeaways: Old passwords are dangerous when people reuse them, so look for reuse.
Valid accounts beat exploits, so watch logins as closely as software flaws.
Keep details about your staff on public sites to the minimum you need.

objectives: List the kinds of technical data that are available for purchase.
Explain the difference between buying data and reading vendor analysis.
Describe how purchased credentials lead to valid account abuse.
Explain why purchase activity is invisible on the victim network.
Outline monitoring for logins that use credentials from known breaches.
